title: Packaging Artwork and Dieline Checklist: Get Print-Ready First Time
seoTitle: Packaging Artwork & Dieline Checklist for Print-Ready Boxes
metaDescription: Bleed, safe zones, CMYK vs Pantone, fonts, barcodes and file formats: a simple checklist to make your box artwork print-ready and avoid costly reprints.
excerpt: Most printing problems start in the artwork file, not on the press. Use this checklist before you send your design and your boxes come out the way you pictured them.
coverAlt: Box dieline with fold lines and dimensions for artwork planning

sections.heading: What a dieline is and why you need it first
sections.body:
A dieline is the flat, unfolded template of your box. It shows the outline that will be cut, the lines that will be folded, and every panel: front, back, sides, lid and flaps.

Always design on the dieline from your supplier, not on a template from the internet. Board thickness changes the exact measurements, so a template made for a different board can put your logo across a fold or cut off the edge of your text.

sections.heading: Read the dieline: what each line means
sections.body: Every supplier uses slightly different colours, but the meaning is always the same. Check the legend on your file.
sections.tableCaption: Common dieline lines and their meaning
sections.table:
Line | Usually shown as | What happens there
Cut line | Solid line | The board is cut through
Fold or crease line | Dashed line | The board is folded
Bleed | Line outside the cut | Artwork must extend to here
Safe zone | Line inside the cut | Keep text and logos inside this
Glue area | Shaded panel | No ink here, glue is applied

sections.heading: The print-ready checklist
sections.body: Go through these before you send your file. Each one prevents a common reprint.
sections.table:
Check | Why it matters
Artwork extends 3 mm (1/8 inch) into the bleed | Stops thin white lines at the edges after cutting
Text and logos sit 3-5 mm inside the safe zone | Nothing important gets cut off or lands on a fold
Colour mode is CMYK, brand colours given as Pantone | Screen RGB colours shift when printed
Images are at least 300 dpi at final size | Low resolution prints blurry
Fonts are outlined or embedded | Missing fonts get replaced with the wrong ones
Smallest text is 6 pt or larger | Tiny text blurs, especially on kraft
Barcodes are black on white, at 100% size | Scanners fail on coloured or shrunk barcodes
Dieline is on its own layer, not printed | Otherwise the template lines get printed
File is PDF, AI or EPS with vectors kept | Keeps logos and text sharp at any size

sections.heading: Colours: CMYK, Pantone and why screens lie
sections.body:
Your screen mixes red, green and blue light (RGB). Printers mix cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks (CMYK). Some bright screen colours, especially neon greens, electric blues and vivid oranges, simply cannot be reproduced exactly in CMYK, so they print duller than you expect.

If a colour is central to your brand, give its Pantone number. The printer can then match it closely or use a special ink. And always judge colour on a printed proof or sample, not on your monitor.

On kraft board every colour prints darker, because the brown shows through. Test light colours before committing to a big run.

sections.heading: Plan every panel, not just the front
sections.body:
Customers turn boxes around. Use each panel with a purpose:

Front: logo, product name and the one line that says why it is good.

Sides: variant, size or scent, so the product is easy to find on a shelf.

Back: description, ingredients or materials, instructions, legal text and the barcode.

Inside or under the lid: a thank-you message, social handle or QR code. This is the part people film when they unbox.

Fold the printed dieline into a paper mock-up before approving. It is the fastest way to catch a logo that ends up upside down.

sections.heading: Mistakes that cause reprints
sections.body:
Text too close to a fold or edge.

Artwork that stops at the cut line with no bleed.

RGB colours or low-resolution images pulled from a website.

A barcode placed on a dark background or shrunk to fit.

Forgetting that the lid flap folds over, so its artwork appears the other way up.

None of these are hard to fix, but they are expensive once thousands of boxes are printed. A careful proof check is the cheapest insurance you can buy.

sections.heading: Proofs: your last chance to catch errors
sections.body:
Before production we send a digital proof: your artwork on the dieline, exactly as it will print. Check spelling, contact details, barcodes and the position of every element. Once you approve the proof, production starts, so take a few minutes over it.

If colour matters a lot, ask for a physical sample as well.

faqs.question: What is a dieline in packaging?
faqs.answer: A dieline is the flat, unfolded template of a box that shows where the board will be cut, folded and glued. Artwork must be designed on the dieline for the exact board being used.

faqs.question: How much bleed does packaging artwork need?
faqs.answer: Usually 3 mm (about 1/8 inch) beyond the cut line on every side, so no white edges appear after cutting.

faqs.question: Should my packaging artwork be CMYK or RGB?
faqs.answer: CMYK. Printers use CMYK inks, so RGB files shift in colour. Give Pantone numbers for important brand colours.

faqs.question: Which file format is best for packaging artwork?
faqs.answer: A print-ready PDF, or an AI or EPS file, with fonts outlined, images at 300 dpi and the dieline on a separate layer.
